title: Inelastic Collisions in One Dimension
lead: When two objects collide and stick together, or when a spring between them lets go, the internal kinetic energy of the pair changes even though its momentum does not. This section names the inelastic collision and the perfectly inelastic collision, uses conservation of momentum on its own to find the velocity two objects share once they have stuck together, and works out how much kinetic energy the collision took away or gave.
objectives: Apply an understanding of collisions to sports.
Determine recoil velocity and loss in kinetic energy given mass and initial velocity.
summary_html:
• An inelastic collision is one in which the internal kinetic energy changes (it is not conserved).
  • A collision in which the objects stick together is sometimes called perfectly inelastic because it reduces internal kinetic energy more than does any other type of inelastic collision.
  • Sports science and technologies also use physics concepts such as momentum and rotational motion and vibrations.
notes: Problems 2, 4, 6, 9, 11 and 13 have no answer in the book’s key and are left out, and part (e) of problem 8, which the key does not cover, is named in its solution rather than asked as a part.
exercise_notes: Bloom levels, concept tags, weights and hints are AI-generated. Answers come from the book’s answer key; problems 2, 4, 6, 9, 11 and 13 have no keyed answer and are left out. The section’s first two AP items ask for the two final velocities of an elastic collision and its ninth gives one final velocity of a collision in which the objects do not stick together, all three of which turn on what section 8.4 introduces, so they are set there instead with source_section 8.5. Nine of section 8.4’s AP items turn on an inelastic or a perfectly inelastic collision, which this section introduces, so they are set here with source_section 8.4. Two of them ask for the velocity of the center of mass of the colliding pair; they stay with their collision, their suggested approaches lean on section 8.3’s sentence that the total momentum of a system is the momentum of its center of mass, and both are tagged with section 6.5’s center of mass. They carry no cite, since this section’s own text never mentions the center of mass. Problem 3 takes the mass and speed of the football player and the football from section 8.1 and stays here, with the book’s reference to that section kept as plain text. The unkeyed conceptual questions and AP items are kept as open items with an AI-marked suggested approach.

figures.original_caption: An inelastic one-dimensional two-object collision. Momentum is conserved, but internal kinetic energy is not conserved. (a) Two objects of equal mass initially head directly toward one another at the same speed. (b) The objects stick together (a perfectly inelastic collision), and so their final velocity is zero. The internal kinetic energy of the system changes in any inelastic collision and is reduced to zero in this example.

exercises.prompt: What is an inelastic collision? What is a perfectly inelastic collision?

answer.solution: An inelastic collision is one in which the internal kinetic energy of the system changes: the forces between the colliding objects do work that removes internal kinetic energy, usually as heat transfer and sound, or that adds to it from energy that was stored. Momentum is still conserved, because the forces between the objects are internal to the system. A perfectly inelastic collision is the special case in which the objects stick together and leave with one velocity between them. It is called perfect because it reduces the internal kinetic energy to the least it can be while momentum is still conserved.

exercises.prompt: Mixed-pair ice skaters performing in a show are standing motionless at arms length just before starting a routine. They reach out, clasp hands, and pull themselves together by only using their arms. Assuming there is no friction between the blades of their skates and the ice, what is their velocity after their bodies meet?

answer.solution: Their velocity is zero. With no friction from the ice, the net external force on the pair of skaters is zero, so the pair is an isolated system and its total momentum cannot change. The two skaters begin at rest, so the total momentum is zero to start with and is still zero when they meet. The forces their arms exert are internal to the system and cancel in pairs, so however hard they pull, the two of them together cannot set themselves moving; they simply come together at the point where they started.

exercises.prompt: A small pickup truck that has a camper shell slowly coasts toward a red light with negligible friction. Two dogs in the back of the truck are moving and making various inelastic collisions with each other and the walls. What is the effect of the dogs on the motion of the center of mass of the system (truck plus entire load)? What is their effect on the motion of the truck?

answer.solution: The dogs have no effect at all on the motion of the center of mass. Friction is negligible, so the net external force on the system of the truck and everything it carries is zero and its total momentum is conserved. Section 8.3 notes that the total momentum is the momentum of the center of mass of the system, so the center of mass keeps coasting at the same velocity however the dogs collide, since every force between a dog and a wall or between the two dogs is internal to the system and is matched by an equal and opposite force. The truck itself is another matter. It is only part of the system, so a dog that pushes off the front wall pushes the truck forward and a dog that strikes the back wall slows it, and the truck speeds up and slows down slightly as the dogs move about. The changes cancel in the long run, because the center of mass of the whole load goes on as before.

exercises.prompt: Mass A (2.0 kg) is moving with an initial velocity of 15 m/s in the +x-direction, and it collides with mass B (5.0 kg), initially at rest. After the collision, the two objects stick together and move as one. What is the change in kinetic energy of the system as a result of the collision?

options: no change
decrease by 225 J
decrease by 161 J
decrease by 64 J
answer.hint: The objects stick together, so conservation of momentum alone gives the one velocity they share afterwards; then compare the kinetic energy before with the kinetic energy after.
answer.solution: (c). Because of conservation of momentum, the final velocity of the combined mass must be 4.286 m/s. The initial kinetic energy is $(0.5)(2.0)(15)^2 = 225\ \text{J}$. The final kinetic energy is $(0.5)(7.0)(4.286)^2 = 64\ \text{J}$, so the difference is −161 J.

exercises.prompt: Mass A (2.0 kg) is moving with an initial velocity of 15 m/s in the +x-direction, and it collides with mass B (4.0 kg), initially moving 7.0 m/s in the +x-direction. After the collision, the two objects stick together and move as one. What is the change in kinetic energy of the system as a result of the collision?

answer.solution: The collision is perfectly inelastic, so begin with conservation of momentum. The total momentum before the collision is $m_1\kvone + m_2\kvtwo$, and after the collision the two masses move as one of mass $m_1 + m_2$, so $m_1\kvone + m_2\kvtwo = (m_1 + m_2)\kvprime$ gives the velocity they share. With that velocity in hand, work out the internal kinetic energy before the collision as $\tfrac{1}{2}m_1\kvone^2 + \tfrac{1}{2}m_2\kvtwo^2$ and after it as $\tfrac{1}{2}(m_1 + m_2)\kvprime^2$, and subtract the first from the second. The difference is negative, as it must be for a perfectly inelastic collision, and it is smaller here than in the previous item because the two objects were already moving the same way and so approached each other slowly.

exercises.prompt: Mass A slides across a rough table with an initial velocity of 12 m/s in the +x-direction. By the time mass A collides with mass B (a stationary object with equal mass), mass A has slowed to 10 m/s. After the collision, the two objects stick together and move as one. Immediately after the collision, the velocity of the system is measured to be 5 m/s in the +x-direction, and the system eventually slides to a stop. Which of the following statements is true about this motion?

options: Momentum is conserved during the collision, but it is not conserved during the motion before and after the collision.
Momentum is not conserved at any time during this analysis.
Momentum is conserved at all times during this analysis.
Momentum is not conserved during the collision, but it is conserved during the motion before and after the collision.
answer.hint: Momentum is conserved while the net external force on the system is zero. Ask when friction from the table is acting and when the forces at work are internal to the two objects.

exercises.prompt: Mass A is initially moving with a velocity of 12 m/s in the +x-direction. Mass B is twice as massive as mass A and is initially at rest. After the two objects collide, the two masses move together as one with a velocity of 4 m/s in the +x-direction. Is momentum conserved in this collision?

answer.solution: Yes. Write the total momentum before the collision and after it and compare them. Before, only mass A is moving, so the total is $m(12\ \text{m/s})$, where $m$ is the mass of A. After, the two move as one body of mass $3m$ at 4 m/s, so the total is $3m(4\ \text{m/s}) = m(12\ \text{m/s})$. The two totals are the same, whatever the value of $m$, so momentum is conserved, which is what we expect when the only forces acting during the collision are the forces the two objects exert on each other. The internal kinetic energy is not conserved: the objects stick together, so this is a perfectly inelastic collision and most of the kinetic energy has gone to heat transfer and sound.

exercises.prompt: Mass A is initially moving with a velocity of 24 m/s in the +x-direction. Mass B is twice as massive as mass A and is initially at rest. The two objects experience a totally inelastic collision. What is the final speed of both objects after the collision?

options: A is not moving; B is moving 24 m/s in the +x-direction.
Neither A nor B is moving.
A is moving 24 m/s in the –x-direction. B is not moving.
Both A and B are moving together 8 m/s in the +x-direction.
answer.hint: In a totally inelastic collision the two objects leave with one velocity between them, so $\kvprime = m_1\kvone/(m_1 + m_2)$ with $m_2 = 2m_1$.

exercises.prompt: Mass A is initially moving with some unknown velocity in the +x-direction. Mass B is twice as massive as mass A and initially at rest. The two objects collide, and after the collision, they move together with a speed of 6 m/s in the +x-direction. (a) Is this collision elastic or inelastic? Explain. (b) Determine the initial velocity of mass A.

answer.solution: (a) The collision is inelastic, and in fact perfectly inelastic, because the two objects move together afterwards. A collision in which the objects stick together reduces the internal kinetic energy more than any other kind can while still conserving momentum, so the internal kinetic energy is certainly not conserved and the collision cannot be elastic. (b) Momentum is conserved, so take the total before the collision, $m\kvone$ with $m$ the mass of A, and set it equal to the total after, $3m(6\ \text{m/s})$. The mass cancels and $\kvone$ follows, three times the final speed and in the same direction. Check the answer by working out the internal kinetic energy before and after: the loss should be the two thirds of the original that a perfectly inelastic collision with a stationary target twice the mass always takes.

exercises.prompt: Mass A is initially moving with a velocity of 15 m/s in the +x-direction. Mass B is twice as massive and is initially moving with a velocity of 10 m/s in the –x-direction. The two objects collide, and after the collision, mass A moves with a speed of 15 m/s in the –x-direction. (a) What is the final velocity of mass B after the collision? (b) Calculate the change in kinetic energy as a result of the collision, assuming mass A is 5.0 kg.

answer.solution: (a) The objects do not stick together here, so use conservation of momentum with four velocities: $m_1\kvone + m_2\kvtwo = m_1\kvoneprime + m_2\kvtwoprime$, where $m_2 = 2m_1$, $\kvone = +15\ \text{m/s}$, $\kvtwo = -10\ \text{m/s}$ and $\kvoneprime = -15\ \text{m/s}$. The only unknown is $\kvtwoprime$; solve for it and note the sign, which says which way B is going. (b) With $m_1 = 5.0\ \text{kg}$ and so $m_2 = 10\ \text{kg}$, work out $\kKEint = \tfrac{1}{2}m_1\kvone^2 + \tfrac{1}{2}m_2\kvtwo^2$ before the collision and $\kKEintprime = \tfrac{1}{2}m_1\kvoneprime^2 + \tfrac{1}{2}m_2\kvtwoprime^2$ after it, and subtract. A negative result means the collision took internal kinetic energy away, as an inelastic collision does; the answer here is small compared with the energy the two objects brought, so this collision is nearly elastic.

exercises.prompt: Two cars (A and B) of mass 1.5 kg collide. Car A is initially moving at 12 m/s, and car B is initially moving in the same direction with a speed of 6 m/s. The two cars are moving along a straight line before and after the collision. What will be the change in momentum of this system after the collision?

options: −27 kg • m/s
zero
+27 kg • m/s
It depends on whether the collision is elastic or inelastic.
answer.hint: The question asks for the momentum of the system, not of one car, and the forces the two cars exert on each other are internal to that system.

exercises.prompt: Two cars (A and B) of mass 1.5 kg collide. Car A is initially moving at 24 m/s, and car B is initially moving in the opposite direction with a speed of 12 m/s. The two cars are moving along a straight line before and after the collision. (a) If the two cars have an elastic collision, calculate the change in momentum of the two-car system. (b) If the two cars have a completely inelastic collision, calculate the change in momentum of the two-car system.

answer.solution: Both answers are zero, and the point of the question is that the same answer comes out twice. The system is the two cars together, the forces between them during the collision are internal to that system, and no external force acts along the line of motion, so the total momentum is the same before and after. Add the two momenta before the collision, $m(24\ \text{m/s}) + m(-12\ \text{m/s})$ with $m = 1.5\ \text{kg}$, and you have the total the system must still carry afterwards, whether the cars bounce apart elastically or stick together. What the kind of collision does decide is how that total is shared between the two cars, and how much internal kinetic energy is left: an elastic collision keeps all of it and a completely inelastic one keeps only what the pair needs to go on moving together.

exercises.prompt: Two objects, A and B, have equal mass. Prior to the collision, mass A is moving 10 m/s in the +x-direction, and mass B is moving 4 m/s in the +x-direction. Which of the following results represents an inelastic collision between A and B?

options: After the collision, mass A is at rest, and mass B moves 14 m/s in the +x-direction.
After the collision, mass A moves 4 m/s in the –x-direction, and mass B moves 18 m/s in the +x-direction.
After the collision, the two masses stick together and move 7 m/s in the +x-direction.
After the collision, mass A moves 4 m/s in the +x-direction, and mass B moves 10 m/s in the +x-direction.
answer.hint: Every option keeps the total momentum the same, so the one that is inelastic is the one in which the internal kinetic energy, the sum of the two kinetic energies, has changed.

exercises.prompt: Two objects of equal mass collide. Object A is initially moving in the +x-direction with a speed of 12 m/s, and object B is initially at rest. After the collision, object A is at rest, and object B is moving away with some unknown velocity. There are no external forces acting on the system of two masses. What statement can we make about this collision?

options: Both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved.
Momentum is conserved, but kinetic energy is not conserved.
Neither momentum nor kinetic energy is conserved.
More information is needed in order to determine which is conserved.
answer.hint: Conservation of momentum fixes the velocity object B leaves with; once you have it, add up the kinetic energies before and after and compare.

exercises.prompt: Two objects of equal mass collide. Object A is initially moving with a velocity of 15 m/s in the +x-direction, and object B is initially at rest. After the collision, object A is at rest. There are no external forces acting on the system of two masses. (a) Use momentum conservation to deduce the velocity of object B after the collision. (b) Is this collision elastic? Justify your answer.

answer.solution: (a) No external force acts, so the total momentum is the same before and after. Before the collision only A is moving, so the total is $m(15\ \text{m/s})$; after the collision only B is moving, so the total is $m\kvtwoprime$ with the same mass $m$. The mass cancels and B leaves with the velocity A came in with, in the same direction. (b) It is elastic. Work out the internal kinetic energy before, $\tfrac{1}{2}m(15\ \text{m/s})^2$, and after, $\tfrac{1}{2}m\kvtwoprime^2$ with the velocity found in part (a). The two are equal, so no internal kinetic energy was lost, which is what an elastic collision means. Two objects of equal mass exchanging velocities in this way is the standard result for a one-dimensional elastic collision.

exercises.prompt: Which of the following statements is true about an inelastic collision?

options: Momentum is conserved, and kinetic energy is conserved.
Momentum is conserved, and kinetic energy is not conserved.
Momentum is not conserved, and kinetic energy is conserved.
Momentum is not conserved, and kinetic energy is not conserved.
answer.hint: Momentum is conserved whenever the net external force on the system is zero; what makes a collision inelastic is what happens to the internal kinetic energy.

exercises.prompt: Explain how the momentum and kinetic energy of a system of two colliding objects changes as a result of (a) an elastic collision and (b) an inelastic collision.

answer.solution: (a) In an elastic collision neither changes. The forces the two objects exert on each other are internal to the system, so with no net external force the total momentum after the collision is the same as before, and an elastic collision is defined as one that also conserves internal kinetic energy, the sum of the two kinetic energies. What does change is how each is shared: the individual momenta and kinetic energies are different afterwards, and only the totals are the same. (b) In an inelastic collision the total momentum is still unchanged, for the same reason, but the internal kinetic energy is not. The work the internal forces do turns some of it into heat transfer and sound, and if the objects stick together the collision is perfectly inelastic and takes away as much as conservation of momentum allows. Stored energy can go the other way: when a compressed spring is released during the collision, the system ends with more internal kinetic energy than it began with, and the collision is inelastic in that direction.

exercises.prompt: Mass A (1.0 kg) slides across a frictionless surface with a velocity of 8 m/s in the positive direction. Mass B (3.0 kg) is initially at rest. The two objects collide and stick together. What will be the change in the center-of-mass velocity of the system as a result of the collision?

options: There will be no change in the center-of-mass velocity.
The center-of-mass velocity will decrease by 2 m/s.
The center-of-mass velocity will decrease by 6 m/s.
The center-of-mass velocity will decrease by 8 m/s.
answer.hint: Section 8.3 says that the total momentum of a system is the momentum of its center of mass, and the surface is frictionless.

exercises.prompt: Mass A (1.0 kg) slides across a frictionless surface with a velocity of 4 m/s in the positive direction. Mass B (1.0 kg) slides across the same surface in the opposite direction with a velocity of −8 m/s. The two objects collide and stick together after the collision. Predict how the center-of-mass velocity will change as a result of the collision, and explain your prediction. Calculate the center-of-mass velocity of the system both before and after the collision and explain why it remains the same or why it has changed.

answer.solution: Predict that it does not change at all. The surface is frictionless, so the net external force on the two objects together is zero and the total momentum is conserved; section 8.3 notes that the total momentum is the momentum of the center of mass of the system, so the center of mass carries on at whatever velocity it already had, straight through the collision. To check it, divide the total momentum by the total mass. Before the collision the total momentum is $m_1\kvone + m_2\kvtwo = (1.0\ \text{kg})(4\ \text{m/s}) + (1.0\ \text{kg})(-8\ \text{m/s})$ and the total mass is 2.0 kg, which gives the center-of-mass velocity. After the collision the two stick together, so the one velocity they share is the same quotient, and the center of mass moves with them. The reason it stays the same is that the forces that act during the collision are internal: whatever momentum one object gains the other loses, so the sum cannot change, and neither can the velocity of the center of mass.

exercises.prompt: A 0.240-kg billiard ball that is moving at 3.00 m/s strikes the bumper of a pool table and bounces straight back at 2.40 m/s (80% of its original speed). The collision lasts 0.0150 s. (a) Calculate the average force exerted on the ball by the bumper. (b) How much kinetic energy in joules is lost during the collision? (c) What percent of the original energy is left?

parts.hint: The average force is the change in momentum divided by the time the collision lasts, and the ball comes back the other way, so the two velocities have opposite signs.
Work out $\tfrac{1}{2}m\kv^2$ before and after and subtract; the question asks how much was lost, so give the size of the difference.
The speed after is 80% of the speed before, and the kinetic energy goes as the square of the speed.

answer.solution: (a) 86.4 N perpendicularly away from the bumper (b) 0.389 J (c) 64.0%

exercises.prompt: Professional Application Using mass and speed data from Linear Momentum and Force and assuming that the football player catches the ball with his feet off the ground with both of them moving horizontally, calculate: (a) the final velocity if the ball and player are going in the same direction and (b) the loss of kinetic energy in this case. (c) Repeat parts (a) and (b) for the situation in which the ball and the player are going in opposite directions. Might the loss of kinetic energy be related to how much it hurts to catch the pass?

parts.hint: Section 8.1 gives a 110-kg player running at 8.00 m/s and a 0.410-kg football thrown at 25.0 m/s. The player catches the ball, so the collision is perfectly inelastic: $m_1\kvone + m_2\kvtwo = (m_1 + m_2)\kvprime$.
Compare $\kKEintprime$ with $\kKEint$; the minus sign says the energy was lost.
Now the ball comes the other way, so give its velocity the opposite sign and work the same conservation of momentum equation again.
The two are approaching each other much faster in this case, so much more internal kinetic energy has to go.

answer.solution: (a) 8.06 m/s (b) −56.0 J (c)(i) 7.88 m/s; (ii) −223 J. Catching the pass head-on destroys about four times as much kinetic energy, which is why it hurts more.

exercises.prompt: Professional Application Two piloted satellites approaching one another, at a relative speed of 0.250 m/s, intending to dock. The first has a mass of $4.00 \times 10^{3}\ \text{kg}$, and the second a mass of $7.50 \times 10^{3}\ \text{kg}$. (a) Calculate the final velocity (after docking) by using the frame of reference in which the first satellite was originally at rest. (b) What is the loss of kinetic energy in this inelastic collision? (c) Repeat both parts by using the frame of reference in which the second satellite was originally at rest. Explain why the change in velocity is different in the two frames, whereas the change in kinetic energy is the same in both.

parts.hint: In this frame the second satellite comes in at 0.250 m/s and the first is at rest, so $\kvprime = m_2\kvtwo/(m_1 + m_2)$.
Only the moving satellite has kinetic energy to start with; subtract what the docked pair has afterwards.
Now the lighter satellite is the one that moves, so the same expression gives a smaller share of its speed to the pair.
The energy lost to the internal forces does not depend on which frame you watch from.

answer.solution: (a) 0.163 m/s in the direction of motion of the more massive satellite (b) 81.6 J (c) $8.70 \times 10^{-2}\ \text{m/s}$ in the direction of motion of the less massive satellite, 81.5 J. Because there are no external forces, the velocity of the center of mass of the two-satellite system is unchanged by the collision. The two velocities calculated above are the velocity of the center of mass in each of the two different individual reference frames. The loss in KE is the same in both reference frames because the KE lost to internal forces (heat, friction, etc.) is the same regardless of the coordinate system chosen.

exercises.prompt: Professional Application Space probes may be separated from their launchers by exploding bolts. (They bolt away from one another.) Suppose a 4800-kg satellite uses this method to separate from the 1500-kg remains of its launcher, and that 5000 J of kinetic energy is supplied to the two parts. What are their subsequent velocities using the frame of reference in which they were at rest before separation?

parts.hint: The pair starts at rest, so the total momentum is zero and stays zero: the two momenta after the separation are equal in size and opposite in direction. Write the 5000 J as the sum of the two kinetic energies and solve the pair of equations together.
The lighter piece takes the same momentum and so the greater speed, in the opposite direction.

exercises.prompt: A 0.0250-kg bullet is accelerated from rest to a speed of 550 m/s in a 3.00-kg rifle. The pain of the rifle’s kick is much worse if you hold the gun loosely a few centimeters from your shoulder rather than holding it tightly against your shoulder. (a) Calculate the recoil velocity of the rifle if it is held loosely away from the shoulder. (b) How much kinetic energy does the rifle gain? (c) What is the recoil velocity if the rifle is held tightly against the shoulder, making the effective mass 28.0 kg? (d) How much kinetic energy is transferred to the rifle-shoulder combination? The pain is related to the amount of kinetic energy, which is significantly less in this latter situation. (e) Calculate the momentum of a 110-kg football player running at 8.00 m/s. Compare the player’s momentum with the momentum of a hard-thrown 0.410-kg football that has a speed of 25.0 m/s. Discuss its relationship to this problem.

parts.hint: The rifle and the bullet start at rest together, so their momenta afterwards are equal in size and opposite in direction.
Use $\tfrac{1}{2}m\kv^2$ with the mass of the rifle alone and the recoil velocity from (a).
The same momentum is now shared with the shoulder, so use 28.0 kg in place of 3.00 kg.
The momentum is the same as in (b) but the mass is larger, and the kinetic energy of a given momentum falls as the mass rises.

answer.solution: (a) 4.58 m/s away from the bullet (b) 31.5 J (c) –0.491 m/s (d) 3.38 J. The book’s key stops at (d); part (e) asks you to compare the player’s momentum with the football’s, as Example 8.1 does.

exercises.prompt: Professional Application The Moon’s craters are remnants of meteorite collisions. Suppose a fairly large asteroid that has a mass of $5.00 \times 10^{12}\ \text{kg}$ (about a kilometer across) strikes the Moon at a speed of 15.0 km/s. (a) At what speed does the Moon recoil after the perfectly inelastic collision (the mass of the Moon is $7.36 \times 10^{22}\ \text{kg}$)? (b) How much kinetic energy is lost in the collision? Such an event may have been observed by medieval English monks who reported observing a red glow and subsequent haze about the Moon. (c) In October 2009, NASA crashed a rocket into the Moon, and analyzed the plume produced by the impact. (Significant amounts of water were detected.) Answer part (a) and (b) for this real-life experiment. The mass of the rocket was 2000 kg and its speed upon impact was 9000 km/h. How does the plume produced alter these results?

parts.hint: The collision is perfectly inelastic, so $\kvprime = m_1\kvone/(m_1 + m_2)$, and the Moon is so much the heavier that the sum is very nearly its own mass.
Almost all of the asteroid’s kinetic energy is lost, so work out $\tfrac{1}{2}m\kv^2$ for the asteroid and subtract the very small amount the Moon carries away.
Turn 9000 km/h into metres per second first, then repeat part (a) with the rocket’s mass.
Repeat part (b) with the rocket’s mass and speed.

answer.solution: (a) $1.02 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{m/s}$ (b) $5.63 \times 10^{20}\ \text{J}$ (almost all KE lost) (c) Recoil speed is $6.79 \times 10^{-17}\ \text{m/s}$, energy lost is $6.25 \times 10^{9}\ \text{J}$. The plume will not affect the momentum result because the plume is still part of the Moon system. The plume may affect the kinetic energy result because a significant part of the initial kinetic energy may be transferred to the kinetic energy of the plume particles.

exercises.prompt: What is the speed of a garbage truck that is $1.20 \times 10^{4}\ \text{kg}$ and is initially moving at 25.0 m/s just after it hits and adheres to a trash can that is 80.0 kg and is initially at rest?

answer.hint: The can sticks to the truck, so the collision is perfectly inelastic and $\kvprime = m_1\kvone/(m_1 + m_2)$.

exercises.prompt: (a) During an ice skating performance, an initially motionless 80.0-kg clown throws a fake barbell away. The clown’s ice skates allow her to recoil frictionlessly. If the clown recoils with a velocity of 0.500 m/s and the barbell is thrown with a velocity of 10.0 m/s, what is the mass of the barbell? (b) How much kinetic energy is gained by this maneuver? (c) Where does the kinetic energy come from?

parts.hint: The clown starts at rest, so the total momentum is zero: the barbell’s momentum and the clown’s are equal in size and opposite in direction.
There was no kinetic energy to begin with, so add up what the clown and the barbell have afterwards.

answer.solution: (a) 4.00 kg (b) 210 J (c) The clown does work to throw the barbell, so the kinetic energy comes from the muscles of the clown. The muscles convert the chemical potential energy of ATP into kinetic energy.
